modules.summary: Speculate about digital evidence with modals of deduction and report statements cleanly with accurate backshift.

grammar.name: Modals of deduction: must, might, could, can't
grammar.explanation: Use must when you are almost certain, might or could when something is possible, and can't when you are almost certain it is untrue.
keyPoints: Certain: The update must have broken the app.
Possible: She might be working from home.
Impossible: That can't be the reason they cancelled.
grammar.example: The site is down, so they must be updating the servers; it could also be a network problem.

items.prompt: The site is down. They ___ be updating the servers.
items.explanation: Must expresses strong certainty based on evidence.

items.prompt: That ___ be the reason — the app works fine on other phones.
items.explanation: Can't marks a conclusion you are almost certain is wrong.

items.prompt: Which sentence leaves the possibility open?
items.explanation: Could expresses possibility without certainty.

grammar.name: Reported statements (backshift)
grammar.explanation: When you report speech, shift the tense back one step and adjust pronouns and time expressions; reporting verbs such as claim, admit and warn change the pattern that follows.
keyPoints: 'I will fix it tomorrow.' → She said she would fix it the next day.
Reporting verb + -ing: He admitted breaking the rules.
Reporting verb + to: They warned us not to share the link.
grammar.example: The engineer said the update would take two days, admitted that the testing had been rushed, and warned us not to reinstall.

items.prompt: 'I will fix it tomorrow.' → She said she ___ it the next day.
items.explanation: Will shifts to would in reported speech.

items.prompt: He admitted ___ the rules.
items.explanation: Admit takes the -ing form.

items.prompt: They warned us ___ the link.
items.explanation: Warn + object + (not) to + infinitive.

inputs.title: Tech news: the week in AI
inputs.body: A major video platform has announced that AI-generated clips must now be labelled. The company said the change would take effect within thirty days and admitted that earlier labelling had been inconsistent. Researchers welcomed the move but warned that labels alone will not stop misinformation, because most people share a clip before they read the caption. One campaign group claimed the policy was 'too little, too late', while the platform insisted that it was a first step. A listener asked whether schools should ban smartphones during lessons or teach students how algorithms sort newsfeeds. Both presenters agreed that banning devices alone cannot solve misinformation. One researcher said that teenagers who learnt how clickbait headlines are tested felt far less manipulated online. Before sharing a dramatic clip, they advised listeners to check who first posted it and ask whether a genuine photographer could have missed obvious details.

options: Labels are not enough on their own
questions.answer: Labels are not enough on their own

inputs.title: The price of a free app
inputs.body: Nothing on your phone is free. When an app costs nothing to install, the cost is usually paid in attention or data. A typical free app requests access to location, contacts and microphone, and many users accept without reading the prompt. Regulators have begun to push back: several countries now require plain-language summaries of what an app collects. Yet the strongest protection remains unglamorous. Turn off permissions you do not use. Read the prompt. And remember that a service designed to keep you scrolling is not designed to help you leave. Many users only notice how much data they share when an oddly specific advert appears seconds after a private search. Browser extensions and stricter permission settings can limit passive tracking, yet convenience often wins. Experts point out that reading a two-minute privacy summary before installing a new tool is one of the simplest ways to protect your digital footprint. Free software is rarely truly free; understanding the trade-off lets you decide which platforms actually deserve space on your home screen. When communities demand clearer consent screens, companies have to redesign defaults rather than hiding key controls behind five sub-menus. Beyond personal privacy settings, digital literacy also depends on slowing down emotional reactions. Platforms earn attention when users react instantly to outrage, confusion, or surprise. Taking ten seconds to check whether a startling claim includes an original link, a clear date, and a named source drastically lowers the chance of passing along misinformation. At home and at work, establishing simple boundaries—such as leaving phones out of the bedroom or checking group chats at fixed times—restores deep concentration. Technology serves daily life best when tools wait quietly until we deliberately open them, rather than pulling us into endless scrolling.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main claim?
options: Free apps are paid for with attention or data
questions.answer: Free apps are paid for with attention or data

questions.prompt: What protection does the writer call strongest?

modules.title: Work and education
modules.summary: Choose accurately between gerunds and infinitives after key verbs and report workplace requests and instructions.

grammar.name: Gerunds and infinitives
grammar.explanation: Distinguish verbs followed by -ing (avoid, consider, suggest, enjoy), verbs followed by to-infinitive (manage, afford, decide, refuse), and verbs whose meaning shifts (remember/stop/try).
keyPoints: Verbs like suggest, recommend, avoid, and risk take -ing, never a to-infinitive.
Stop + -ing means quit an activity; stop + to-infinitive means pause in order to do something else.
Remember + -ing looks back at a memory; remember + to-infinitive reminds you of a duty.
grammar.example: She suggested rehearsing the presentation twice before remembering to back up her slides.

items.prompt: Our mentor suggested ___ the workshop notes into three clear actions.
items.explanation: "Suggest" is followed by -ing (or a that-clause), not a to-infinitive.

items.prompt: I stopped ___ emails after eight o’clock so I could sleep properly.
items.explanation: Stop + -ing means giving up or ending the action.

items.prompt: Did you remember ___ the application form before the noon deadline?
items.explanation: Remember + to-infinitive refers to not forgetting a task.

grammar.name: Reported requests and commands
grammar.explanation: Report instructions, advice, and requests cleanly using tell / ask / remind / advise + object + (not) to-infinitive.
keyPoints: Use ask + object + to-infinitive for polite requests: She asked us to send the draft early.
Use tell / instruct + object + not to-infinitive for negative rules.
Never use "say" directly with object + to-infinitive.
grammar.example: The coordinator asked us not to interrupt during the client demo and reminded everyone to mute notifications.

items.prompt: The line manager ___ me to double-check the budget figures.
items.explanation: Ask + object + to-infinitive reports a request; "said me to" is incorrect.

items.prompt: Our tutor told us ___ memorise whole essays word for word.
items.explanation: Negative reported commands place "not" before "to".

items.prompt: The HR adviser reminded new graduates ___ relevant examples in interviews.
items.explanation: Remind takes object + to-infinitive.

inputs.title: First-year mentoring at work and university
inputs.body: Callum: In today’s workplace brief, we are looking at why so many graduates struggle during their first six months in a new role. Maya, you run a mentoring scheme for young technicians. What surprised you most when you started? Maya: Honestly, it was not a lack of technical knowledge. Most apprentices already knew the software. What stressed them out was guessing unwritten expectations. Nobody had ever told them not to spend four hours polishing a routine update, or suggested asking for feedback halfway through a task instead of waiting until Friday. Callum: So clear communication saved time on both sides? Maya: Completely. We started pairing every newcomer with a senior mentor who meets them for twenty minutes each Wednesday. Mentors remind new staff to prioritise urgent jobs, delegate shared admin, and ask questions early. Within one term, fewer people missed deadlines and confidence jumped noticeably.

options: Guessing unwritten expectations about how to work

questions.answer: Short weekly check-ins with an experienced mentor

inputs.title: Beyond exam grades: what employers and tutors value
inputs.body: For decades, university prospectuses and job adverts treated formal grades as the quickest way to compare applicants. While exam scores still show whether someone can absorb demanding material under pressure, hiring managers increasingly look for evidence of how candidates work once a project becomes messy. A recent survey of training coordinators across Britain found that three habits repeatedly set strong candidates apart: asking precise questions early, accepting constructive feedback without becoming defensive, and explaining complex choices clearly to non-specialists. None of these skills requires a specific degree subject. Students build them through part-time work, community volunteering, apprenticeships, and group seminars where deadlines actually matter. One coordinator noted that applicants who avoid admitting mistakes often slow an entire team down, whereas people who flag problems early help everyone adjust before a deadline slips. Practical reflection—asking what worked, what failed, and what to change next week—turns everyday study into genuine professional readiness. Interviews and probation reviews increasingly reflect this shift toward practical problem-solving. Rather than asking candidates to recite textbook definitions, hiring panels frequently present a realistic short scenario: a client has changed priorities two days before a deadline, or a teammate has fallen behind on shared data. Strong applicants explain who they would consult first, what tasks they would delegate or pause, and how they would confirm expectations in writing. At the same time, continuing to read widely and practising formal writing ensures that practical experience rests on clear communication. Combining hands-on adaptability with reflective study prepares learners for both university seminars and collaborative workplaces.

modules.vocabularyTopic: Newsrooms, sources, bias and viral stories

grammar.name: Reporting verbs (admit, deny, suggest, insist)
grammar.explanation: Move beyond "say" and "tell" by matching each reporting verb to its grammatical pattern: verb + -ing (admit, deny, suggest), verb + on + -ing (insist), or verb + to-infinitive (promise, refuse).
keyPoints: Admit, deny, and suggest take -ing (or a that-clause): The editor denied altering the quote.
Insist takes on + -ing or that + clause: She insisted on checking both sources.
Warn and persuade require an object before the to-infinitive.
grammar.example: The presenter denied exaggerating the figures and insisted on publishing the full dataset online.

items.prompt: The journalist admitted ___ an unverified headline too quickly.
items.explanation: "Admit" takes -ing or a that-clause.

items.prompt: The spokesperson insisted ___ reading the complete transcript before commenting.
items.explanation: Insist pairs with the preposition "on" + -ing.

items.prompt: Several readers warned the site ___ confusing opinion columns with news reports.
items.explanation: "Warn someone against + -ing" is a natural B2 structure.

grammar.name: Reported questions
grammar.explanation: Report yes/no questions with if/whether and wh-questions with statement word order (no auxiliary do/did and no question mark).
keyPoints: Use ask / wonder + if or whether for yes/no questions.
Keep subject before verb: She asked where the reporter had found the statistics.
Drop do/does/did and shift tenses back when the reporting verb is in the past.
grammar.example: The host asked the editor whether readers still trusted local radio and how the newsroom checked viral clips.

items.prompt: The interviewer asked the author why ___ the article.
items.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order (subject + verb).

items.prompt: Listeners asked ___ the podcast would release a follow-up episode.
items.explanation: Yes/no reported questions require "if" or "whether".

items.prompt: He wanted to know how long the verification process usually ___.
items.explanation: Backshift present simple to past simple without "did".

inputs.title: Inside a fact-checking desk
inputs.body: Presenter: When a dramatic video goes viral before breakfast, how does a small fact-checking team decide what is genuine? Ananya, you spent three years leading an investigative desk in Mumbai before moving to London. What happens in the first twenty minutes? Ananya: First, we slow down. Last month, a clip claimed a historic bridge had collapsed overnight. Several websites repeated the rumour immediately, though one local council denied any damage had occurred. Our team asked whether any eyewitnesses had posted clear photographs with local street signs, and we checked weather logs from that morning. Presenter: Did the original account admit making a mistake? Ananya: Not at first—they insisted on keeping the post up for clicks, even after engineers confirmed the footage came from an old film set in another region. Eventually, the platform added a warning label and the blog retracted its headline. Listeners asked how ordinary readers can avoid getting caught out. My rule is simple: pause for sixty seconds, check who benefits from your anger, and see whether two independent newsrooms confirm the same details.

questions.prompt: How did Ananya’s team prove the bridge footage was misleading?
options: They deleted the blog’s account immediately
They checked eyewitness street details, weather logs, and the footage origin
They waited three weeks for a TV broadcast
questions.answer: They checked eyewitness street details, weather logs, and the footage origin

questions.prompt: What first step does Ananya recommend to ordinary readers?
options: Pause briefly and see if two independent outlets confirm the claim
Share posts quickly so friends can check them
questions.answer: Pause briefly and see if two independent outlets confirm the claim

inputs.title: Why slow journalism is finding an audience again
inputs.body: For much of the past decade, digital newsrooms raced to publish breaking updates faster than their rivals. Breaking alerts certainly help during emergencies, yet speed-first reporting carries a clear cost: nuances disappear, early rumours get repeated before anyone can verify them, and readers end up exhausted rather than informed. In response, a growing number of weekly newsletters, audio documentaries, and independent magazines have turned toward what editors call slow journalism. Instead of chasing every trending headline, journalists spend weeks interviewing eyewitnesses, checking public budgets, and testing claims against original data. When mistakes occur, transparent outlets admit getting a detail wrong and publish visible corrections rather than quietly editing a paragraph online. Readers appear willing to pay modestly for calmer reporting that respects their time and avoids sensationalising routine disagreements. As one editor put it recently, audiences do not want twenty breathless updates an hour; they want one trustworthy explanation they can still rely on next month. Choosing two or three balanced sources—including outlets outside your usual echo chamber—helps transform passive scrolling into genuinely critical reading. Digital tools have also made it far easier for everyday readers to verify basic claims themselves before reacting. Checking when an image first appeared online, reading past the headline to the original report, and comparing two outlets with different editorial traditions take less than three minutes. Teachers and community libraries increasingly run short workshops showing teenagers and older adults how headlines frame identical statistics in opposite ways. When readers ask "Who collected this sample?" or "What important context is missing?", sensationalised posts lose much of their power. Informed habits on the audience side reward journalists who invest time in accurate, unhurried reporting.

questions.prompt: What downside of speed-first reporting does the article highlight?
options: Audiences refuse to read breaking alerts during emergencies
Rumours spread before verification and nuances get lost
Print newspapers become too expensive to deliver
questions.answer: Rumours spread before verification and nuances get lost

questions.prompt: How do transparent slow-journalism outlets handle errors?
options: They quietly delete the entire article
They admit mistakes openly and publish visible corrections
questions.answer: They admit mistakes openly and publish visible corrections

modules.title: Environment and sustainability
modules.summary: Reflect on past environmental choices with third and mixed conditionals, and express regrets or desired changes with wish / if only.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Climate action, urban heat and sustainability

grammar.name: Conditionals 3 and mixed
grammar.explanation: The third conditional imagines an unreal past; mixed conditionals connect an unreal past to a present result, or a present state to a past result.
keyPoints: Third: If the city had invested earlier, the floods would not have been so severe.
Past → present: If I had studied planning, I would be working on this project now.
Present → past: If she were more patient, she would not have quit.
grammar.example: If the council had built the drainage in 2015, the damage would not be costing us millions now.

items.prompt: If the city had invested earlier, the floods ___ so severe.
items.explanation: Third conditional: had + past participle, would have + past participle.

items.prompt: If I had studied planning, I ___ on this project now.
items.explanation: Mixed conditional: past cause with a present result.

items.prompt: Which sentence blames a past action for a present situation?
options: If we had acted, the park would be open now.
If we act, the park will open.
If we were acting, the park would be open.
items.answer: If we had acted, the park would be open now.
items.explanation: Past perfect in the if-clause plus present result is the mixed pattern.

grammar.name: wish / if only
grammar.explanation: Use wish or if only with the past simple for a present regret, with the past perfect for a past regret, and with would to complain about someone else's behaviour.
keyPoints: Present regret: I wish I lived closer to work.
Past regret: I wish we had started ten years ago.
Complaint: I wish the council would collect the bins on time.
grammar.example: I wish the city had kept the old tram line; if only we could use it now.

items.prompt: I wish I ___ closer to work.
items.explanation: A present regret takes the past simple after wish.

items.prompt: I wish we ___ ten years ago.
items.explanation: A past regret takes the past perfect after wish.

items.prompt: Which sentence complains about someone else's behaviour?
options: I wish I had a bike.
I wish the council would fix the road.
items.answer: I wish the council would fix the road.
items.explanation: Wish + would expresses irritation about another person's action.

inputs.title: Documentary excerpt: the city that cooled itself
inputs.body: In 2019 this square was a car park. Summer temperatures here were four degrees higher than in the park two streets away, an effect researchers call the urban heat island. The city tried something unfashionable: it planted trees, removed the asphalt and put a small fountain where the delivery vans used to park. Four years later, the temperature difference has almost disappeared. The scheme cost less than one kilometre of road. What surprised the engineers was not the cooling, but how quickly residents started using the space. Residents interviewed on the street said they wished earlier planners had protected older trees instead of paving over parks in the nineties. If those green corridors had survived, summer nights would be noticeably cooler right now. Even so, local volunteers remain practical: small shaded pocket parks and reliable trams prove that towns can adapt steadily when citizens and engineers plan together.

options: How quickly residents used the space
questions.answer: How quickly residents used the space

inputs.title: Problem, solution: the heat in our streets
inputs.body: Cities are hotter than the countryside around them, and the difference is not evenly spread. Districts with fewer trees and more asphalt can be five degrees warmer than wealthier, greener neighbours, which means the people least able to afford air conditioning are the ones who need it most. The solutions are unglamorous and well understood: plant mature trees rather than saplings, replace dark surfaces with reflective ones, and open air-conditioned public buildings during heatwaves. The obstacle is rarely knowledge. It is the budget cycle, which rewards visible new projects over invisible maintenance. Look closely at how a few mid-sized cities turned summer complaints into lasting redesigns. Instead of waiting for expensive megaprojects, councils started by painting dark asphalt roofs pale white, planting native street trees outside bus shelters, and converting single car lanes into shaded cycle corridors. Within three summers, ground temperatures dropped and independent cafés reported higher afternoon footfall because people could actually sit outside comfortably. If local authorities had ignored those early pilot schemes, energy bills for air conditioning would now be climbing even faster. Every small adaptation teaches residents what a calmer, greener street feels like—turning abstract climate targets into everyday comfort. Just as importantly, community involvement ensures that green redesigns last beyond a single election cycle. When residents help decide where shaded benches, bike racks, and rainwater gardens go, neighbourhoods protect those spaces as shared assets rather than viewing them as imposed rules. Schoolchildren help water newly planted saplings along walking routes, while local shopkeepers notice calmer streets invite families to linger longer. Critics once worried that removing roadside parking spaces would reduce trade, yet surveys across several European towns showed retail footfall either held steady or rose once crossings felt safer and summer shade improved.

questions.prompt: Who suffers most from urban heat?
options: Districts with fewer trees and less money
questions.answer: Districts with fewer trees and less money

outline.analyze: Purpose: inform and recommend. Audience: residents and local officials. Register: formal, impersonal.
